meta.title: Who really said "Humility is not thinking less of yourself, it's thinking of yourself less"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — C.S. Lewis never wrote this. It's a modern paraphrase of his idea, worded by Howard & Lash (1998) and popularized by Rick Warren's Purpose Driven Life.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Humility is not thinking less of yourself, it's thinking of yourself less'?
meta.ogDescription: Not C.S. Lewis. A modern summary of his teaching, worded by Howard & Lash (1998) and popularized by Rick Warren (2002); a related line dates to Ken Blanchard, 1990.

answer.label: Not Lewis’s words — a modern paraphrase of his idea
answer.authorDates: 1898–1963 · the idea is his; the polished wording is not
answer.sourceLine: This tidy antithesis appears nowhere in Mere Christianity or any other work by Lewis. It is a modern summary of his teaching that humility means self-forgetfulness. Nearly identical wording — “Real humility is not thinking less of ourselves; it is thinking of ourselves less” — is documented in Rick Howard & Jamie Lash’s 1998 This Was Your Life! and was popularized by Rick Warren’s 2002 The Purpose Driven Life; a related aphorism was credited to Ken Blanchard as early as 1990.

source.excerpt: Humility is not thinking less of yourself, it’s thinking of yourself less.
trail: The C.S. Lewis Foundation lists this line among quotes NOT written by Lewis, tracing it instead to Rick Warren or to Rick Howard & Jamie Lash.
Etymologist Barry Popik’s chronology finds the earliest kindred line in a March 1990 Democrat and Chronicle crediting Ken Blanchard: “Don’t think less of yourself, just think of yourself less.”

Christianity Today notes the near-exact wording — “Real humility is not thinking less of ourselves; it is thinking of ourselves less” — appears in Howard & Lash’s 1998 This Was Your Life!, which then quotes Lewis in the next breath.
Check Your Fact confirms the sentence appears nowhere in Mere Christianity or any other Lewis work.
source.excerptNote: What Lewis actually wrote, in the chapter “The Great Sin,” is that the truly humble man “will not be thinking about himself at all” — the self-forgetfulness half of the popular line, without its neat “not thinking less of yourself” antithesis.

source.rightsNote: The line is not from a pre-1931 public-domain text. Its memorable modern wording is documented in Rick Howard & Jamie Lash’s This Was Your Life! (1998) and Rick Warren’s The Purpose Driven Life (Zondervan, 2002) — both firmly in copyright. Because no single originating work can be pinned with certainty, treat the phrasing as a modern, in-copyright coinage rather than a public-domain quotation.

author.name: C.S. Lewis
author.heading: C.S. Lewis
author.metaLine: 1898–1963 · Oxford & Cambridge scholar, author of Mere Christianity
author.bio: Clive Staples Lewis was a British literary scholar and Christian apologist, best known for Mere Christianity, The Screwtape Letters, and The Chronicles of Narnia. In the Mere Christianity chapter “The Great Sin,” he described genuine humility as self-forgetfulness — the humble man “will not be thinking about himself at all.” That idea is the seed later writers compressed into the popular antithesis, which is why his name keeps getting attached to words he never actually wrote.

misattribution.heading: How Lewis got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most common quotations falsely pinned on C.S. Lewis. The sentence is a modern paraphrase of his teaching, not a line he wrote.

items.why: It appears in no Lewis book, essay, or letter. The C.S. Lewis Foundation lists it explicitly among quotes not by Lewis, and Check Your Fact confirms it is not in Mere Christianity.

items.who: Rick Howard & Jamie Lash / Rick Warren
items.why: The near-exact form is in Howard & Lash’s 1998 This Was Your Life!, which quotes Lewis in the following sentence; Rick Warren then rephrased and popularized it in The Purpose Driven Life (2002), without crediting Lewis. That summary-plus-Lewis-quote sequence is how the two got conflated.

Per Barry Popik’s research, a March 1990 Democrat and Chronicle article credited management writer Ken Blanchard with “Don’t think less of yourself, just think of yourself less” — a distinct but kindred aphorism.

misattribution.truthLine: The polished antithesis is a modern paraphrase of Lewis’s point that humility is self-forgetfulness — not a sentence he ever wrote. See the Christianity Today account.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: Lewis really did teach a version of this. In the Mere Christianity chapter “The Great Sin,” he argued that a genuinely humble person is not self-abasing but self-forgetful — someone who “will not be thinking about himself at all.” The popular quotation captures that spirit almost perfectly, which is exactly why it feels like something Lewis would have said.

The wording that circulates, though, is a later compression. Writers summarizing Lewis’s idea set their paraphrase right next to a genuine Lewis quotation, and over time the paraphrase absorbed his name. The result is a saying that is true to Lewis’s thought but not to his pen.
detailsBody: In “The Great Sin,” Lewis writes that if you met a truly humble man you would think him a cheerful, intelligent person who took a real interest in you — and that “he will not be thinking about himself at all.” That is the authentic root of the popular line, minus its tidy “not thinking less of yourself” framing.
context.pull: The idea is Lewis’s. The sentence is not.
